A radio telescope records a narrow streak across a plot of frequency and time. It could be worth another observation. It could also be interference from equipment much closer to home. A model can move that streak to the front of a scientist's queue; establishing where it came from takes a different kind of work.

That distinction runs through AI in the search for extraterrestrial life. Researchers use machine learning to reject radio interference, examine planet candidates, estimate atmospheric properties and choose where to collect a sample. These systems work on different evidence, from telescope observations to laboratory measurements and simulated spectra. None has established that life exists beyond Earth: NASA's account of the search still describes an open scientific question.

For an engineer, the useful story is in the machinery: which teams have a concrete task, what goes into their models, what comes out, and which data and software are available to inspect. This overview follows that chain through three branches of the search. Readers looking for a starting point can jump to the dataset and tool comparison . It draws on published research and project documentation checked in October 2026; DataRoot Labs has not reproduced these experiments.

## Three searches, different kinds of evidence

SETI , the search for extraterrestrial intelligence, looks for technosignatures : potentially observable evidence of technology. Radio transmissions are one possibility; unusual infrared emissions are another. Biosignatures concern life more broadly, including microbial life. A chemical pattern can be interesting without pointing to an intelligent civilization.

Exoplanet research sits alongside both. Finding a planet and estimating its atmosphere helps researchers decide what to investigate, but neither step establishes that the planet is inhabited.

## Machine learning in SETI: finding the signals worth revisiting

### Radio interference is part of the dataset

A radio spectrogram is an image with time on one axis, frequency on the other and signal strength represented by intensity. Terrestrial transmitters create abundant structure in these images. A useful search must distinguish promising patterns from that background without throwing away the signal it hopes to find.

One way to test a candidate is to alternate between pointing at a target and pointing elsewhere. A signal associated with the target should behave differently from interference that remains visible across pointings. The UCLA SETI group's direction-of-origin model uses a convolutional neural network to examine those relationships. Its repository contains code and a demonstration notebook; the README links separately to test data and trained weights on Dryad. The Zenodo release archives the software.

This is a useful example of a scientific question shaping the learning task. The network is assessing consistency across observations. It is not trained on a collection of confirmed extraterrestrial transmissions; no such positive examples have been established.

### Eight candidates, and the importance of a second look

In a 2023 Nature Astronomy study , Peter Ma and collaborators analyzed Breakthrough Listen's Green Bank Telescope observations of 820 stars. Their system combined a variational autoencoder, which learns a compact representation of an input, with a random-forest classifier. Training used simulated signals against observational backgrounds.

The search identified eight signals of interest. Follow-up observations have so far not redetected them. The result demonstrates a way to sift observations and select candidates; it does not establish eight extraterrestrial sources.

The comparison also needs a strong conventional baseline. A later preprint by Painter and colleagues reported recovering candidates previously identified by both machine-learning and classical searches using a low-complexity statistical process. That makes “AI found what traditional methods cannot” a poor general description of this field.

### Clustering can reduce the review queue

GLOBULAR , published in The Astronomical Journal in 2025, approaches the problem through the properties of detected signals. It uses HDBSCAN, a clustering method that can group dense regions without assigning every point to a cluster, to help remove radio-frequency interference.

The authors reanalyzed Green Bank observations of 97 nearby galaxies that had previously been searched with turboSETI alone, a standard narrowband signal-detection pipeline. They reported reductions of 93.1% in false-positive hits and 99.3% in false-positive events . A hit is a detection in one observation; an event links detections across the on/off-target sequence. These percentages measure unwanted candidates removed from those observations.

There was a sensitivity cost: turboSETI alone recovered 86 of 100 injected synthetic events, versus 69 after clustering. This test used strong, deliberately constructed signals; the counts do not establish sensitivity to every signal a telescope might encounter.

For a team implementing a comparable search, the practical question is how much human review remains at a measured sensitivity to injected signals. That is more informative than a classifier accuracy measured on a conveniently balanced test set.

## Infrared technosignatures: when an interesting source is a background galaxy

The idea behind a Dyson-sphere search is that large-scale energy use might produce detectable waste heat. Astronomers therefore examine stars with unusual infrared emission, while checking ordinary sources of that excess.

Project Hephaistos II combined Gaia, 2MASS and WISE data in a search across roughly five million objects. A convolutional network helped filter image contamination; additional cuts produced seven candidate M-dwarf systems in the 2024 study. The neural network was one stage in a larger astronomical analysis.

Follow-up illustrates why the images matter. A July 2026 JWST preprint attributes the excess around candidates D and E to background galaxies. A separate archival analysis accepted by MNRAS reports strong evidence of contamination for B and C. These findings concern particular candidates; they should not be flattened into a verdict about every object in the original list.

Candidate D shows why resolution matters. The archival study found no obvious sign of contamination there, yet JWST resolved a background galaxy within about one arcsecond of the star. An unusual catalog measurement can come from two objects blended together, and the follow-up is the result readers need alongside the candidate count.

## AI in astronomy: from planet candidates to atmospheric spectra

### NASA's ExoMiner++ vets transit candidates

When a planet passes in front of its star, the measured brightness can dip. Other processes, including eclipsing stars and instrumental effects, can produce confusing patterns. Vetting asks which candidate signals warrant a planetary interpretation.

NASA's ExoMiner++ applies deep learning to that task with data from TESS. NASA's 2026 account describes an initial set of about 7,000 candidates for further study. That number should remain separate from the 370 previously validated Kepler planets associated with the earlier ExoMiner work: candidates and validated planets are different stages.

The NASA repository provides model resources and a documented workflow for preparing inputs and running inference. This gives engineers a more concrete starting point than a discovery headline. The model scores candidate events and their supporting diagnostics, which says nothing yet about a planet's surface conditions.

### Ariel turns atmospheric measurement into a reproducible challenge

A spectrum records light intensity across wavelengths, revealing patterns that depend on atmospheric conditions. Extracting a planet's atmospheric spectrum requires separating a small planetary signal from stellar light and instrument behavior. The Ariel Data Challenge gives researchers a controlled version of that problem using simulated observations for the mission in development.

The 2025 challenge data include simulated detector measurements and calibration information. Participants reconstruct spectra and their uncertainties from simulations of the mission, so every pipeline is scored against known conditions.

It also resists a simple deep-learning narrative. The first-place solution describes a Bayesian-inference approach. A useful survey of AI in science should retain those alternatives: a competition's subject does not determine which method wins.

### Atmospheric retrieval asks an inverse question

Forward modeling predicts a spectrum from an assumed atmosphere. Retrieval works in the other direction: given a spectrum, which atmospheric conditions could have produced it? Several combinations of conditions may fit, so a range of plausible answers is more useful than an unexplained single estimate.

FM4AR proposes a range of atmospheric explanations, including possible temperature profiles. Its neural model learns these distributions through flow matching; a statistical step called importance sampling then reweights the proposals against the spectrum and physical model. The code release and associated synthetic data expose how the method is evaluated. On simulated spectra, the authors report results on a par with nested sampling, the slower conventional approach, and low importance-sampling efficiency flags cases where the neural proposals fail. Both checks work within the chosen physical model, so the quality of that model still bounds the answer.

For rocky planets, INARA DS1 provides approximately 3.1 million synthetic spectra generated with the Planetary Spectrum Generator. The 2025 dataset paper includes a neural-network demonstration using a smaller noiseless subset. Clouds were excluded from the simulations. Those conditions matter when deciding whether a method trained on the collection is ready for a particular telescope observation.

## Biosignatures: chemical patterns and places to sample

### Laboratory chemistry supplies measurable examples

Some biosignature research asks whether mixtures of molecules carry a recognizable imprint of biology, even when an individual molecule is inconclusive.

A 2023 study by Cleaves and colleagues used pyrolysis gas chromatography–mass spectrometry: samples are heated, their components separated, and the resulting chemical fragments measured. A random forest classified 134 samples of biological and non-biological origin with approximately 90% accuracy in the reported experiments.

That is an empirical result on a defined collection of samples. It is not a calibrated 90% chance of identifying unknown extraterrestrial life. The paper's data deposit and the analysis scripts in the repository's master branch are starting points for exam
